items.label: Iran/Hormuz conflict escalating further -- CENTCOM strikes on 5 tankers, Iranian missile attack on US ally Jordan
items.detail: Continued, widening escalation with no ceasefire (live web search, Sept 8-9 sources): CENTCOM destroyed 5 named Iranian crude tankers on Sept 8-9 (Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and Derya near Kharg Island) after the IRGC twice tried to strike a US warship (Al Jazeera, Sept 9). Iran retaliated by firing 20 ballistic missiles at Al Azraq air base in Jordan -- a US ally -- on Sept 9; Jordan says it intercepted 18, two fell in unpopulated areas, no casualties (NBC News/Al Jazeera, Sept 9), marking the conflict's first direct strike on a third-country US ally base. Separately, the new Houthi-Saudi front from Sept 8 (strikes on Aramco facilities and a Saudi air base, 73 wounded) continues. Brent crude rose further to $100.71/bbl on Sept 9 (+2.85% day/day, TradingEconomics/Fortune), crossing $100 for the first time this cycle. The account holds no direct oil & gas exposure but remains 69.38% concentrated in SPY5+SPYL, which would be hit hard by any broad equity selloff or oil-driven inflation surprise, and the account's Canadian mining names (CCJ, KGC) add a second channel of exposure if the conflict pressures global risk sentiment further.
items.recommendation: Do not add to SPY5/SPYL or initiate new discretionary equity purchases while the Iran/Hormuz conflict remains unresolved, especially now that it has directly struck a third-country US-ally base (Jordan) -- a materially higher escalation ladder than tanker/vessel strikes alone. Prioritize the DBC diversification action above (the one true negative-correlation hedge found this run) over the lower-conviction TLT/DBC picks for the other two clusters, since DBC would benefit most directly from continued oil/inflation-driven stress, now that Brent has cleared $100/bbl.

items.label: US-Canada trade war escalating further -- Trump bans Canadian dairy/motorcycles/alcohol imports effective Sept 29
items.detail: New this run (live web search, Sept 7-8 sources): Canada's retaliatory tariffs (15-50% on 700+ US products, ~$20B) took effect Sept 8 as planned, including steel/aluminum duties doubled to 50% (CNN/Al Jazeera). In direct response, Trump issued presidential actions banning imports of Canadian dairy, motorcycles, and alcoholic beverages effective Sept 29 (NPR, Sept 8), and separately reiterated the threatened Bombardier aircraft sales ban and the planned 50% auto-tariff hike from January (Al Jazeera/CNN). No walk-back or negotiation breakthrough reported as of Sept 10 -- trajectory is further escalation, not de-escalation. The account holds two Canadian-headquartered miners, CCJ (Cameco, $10,041.00, 2.06% of NAV) and KGC (Kinross Gold, $8,313.25, 1.71% of NAV), combined $18,354.25 = 3.77% of NAV -- a genuine, if secondary, exposure channel to cross-border trade friction on top of the commodity-price risk already flagged in the materials-satellites item above.
items.recommendation: No action needed at the current 3.77%-of-NAV combined exposure, but do not add to CCJ or KGC while the tariff dispute is actively escalating; the new Sept 29 dairy/motorcycle/alcohol import ban does not directly target uranium or gold, but watch for any Canada-specific mineral-export retaliation before the next review given the pattern of escalation on both sides.
